extracted.intended_audience: military administrators, Judge Advocate/legal officers, and War Department officials handling desertion, rewards, and pay issues
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal standards and administrative rules governing liability for expenses, payment of rewards, evidentiary rules, restoration, punishment, and pay consequences in cases of military desertion under Army regulations and precedent. Focused on when rewards/expenses may be charged, withheld, reimbursed, or paid and related procedural/evidentiary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to charge deserter with transportation expense (par. 127 A.R. 1910)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 127, Army Regulations 1910, provides that 'a soldier convicted by a court-martial of absence without leave will be charged with the expense incurred in transporting him to his proper station.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authorizes a stoppage for transportation and commutation of rations for himself and the guard sent after him (citing multiple Comptroller/Attorney General rulings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification agent transport costs chargeable as apprehension expense
rubrics_metrics.description: A sergeant sent to identify a deserter (supposed serving under assumed name) is not a 'witness' within paragraph 127, and thus the cost of his transportation is, under that paragraph, a proper charge against the deserter as expenses paid for apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuit expenses by enlisted men chargeable even if wrong man
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses incurred by enlisted men in the pursuit of a particular deserter, and therefore on account of his desertion, may properly be charged against him under paragraph 127 notwithstanding that the person apprehended proved to be the wrong man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil officer entitled to reward for arrest and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil officer who arrested a deserter and turned him over to a detachment sent in pursuit is entitled to the reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also held that transportation from place of delivery to station or place of trial is a distinct charge not included in reward and will be set against pay upon conviction. Cases: G. 3405 July 29, 1897; 17847 June 7, 1911.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation to proper station must follow shortest usual route
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement of regulations that a deserter be charged with cost of returning him to his station contemplates travel from place of apprehension/delivery to his proper station by the shortest usually traveled route.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sent by a non-shortest route, cost of that journey not contemplated by regulation and apportionment should be determined by circumstances. Case: C. 17847 Sept. 2, 1908.

rubrics_metrics.name: No liability for rewards/expenses if acquitted or conviction disapproved
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier charged with desertion is acquitted, or where, if convicted, his conviction is disapproved by competent reviewing authority, he cannot legally be made liable for the amount of a reward paid or payable for his arrest as a deserter since he is not a deserter in law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple precedents: R. 26, 347 July 1868; C. 9628 Jan. 3, 1901; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenses not chargeable if conviction disapproved (equivalent to acquittal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter is not chargeable with the expenses of transportation of himself and guard if his conviction has been duly disapproved; such disapproval is tantamount to an acquittal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited rulings: R. 50, 105 Mar. 1886; C. 2121 Mar. 1896; 9540 Jan. 3, 1901; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation incurred in execution of sentence borne by United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of transportation of a convicted deserter, incurred in the course of execution of his sentence, is not chargeable against the deserter under par. 127 but must be borne by the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: When stoppage of pay for reward is authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoppage against the pay of a soldier of the amount due as a reward for his apprehension is authorized (a) upon conviction of desertion; (b) upon restoration to duty without trial if desertion is admitted; (c) upon being brought to trial and convicted of absence without leave if sentence directs stoppage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation paragraphs cited across years. If charge dropped as erroneous, stoppage should be removed as unauthorized. Case: C. 17327 July 18, 1907.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenses incurred without military request not chargeable to soldier
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier was arrested by a peace officer in mistaken belief that he was a deserter, and expenses were incurred for his support without request of military authority, such expenses cannot lawfully be stopped against the soldier's pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer of reward becomes binding only on substantial performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Under contract law, the offer of a reward is an offer of a promise for an act and becomes binding upon substantial performance of the act; part performance only gives no claim for compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: R. 20 Mar. 1866; 17327A Dec. 17, 1908. Citations to contract treatises.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reward if deserter serving in another branch at time of arrest
rubrics_metrics.description: No reward will be paid where the deserter, at the time of arrest, 'is serving in some other branch of the Army' (i.e., has effectively re-enlisted elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reward not payable for arrest of deserter from Cavalry serving in Infantry at arrest. Cases cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reward/allowance for unsolicited detective agency information
rubrics_metrics.description: Information furnished without request by a detective agency that a deserter was serving elsewhere does not entitle the agency to reward or allowance for time/expenses incurred in search.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reward where deserter has contracted new status in other service
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deserter subsequently enlisted in another service (e.g., Marine Corps) and thereby contracted a new status which is voidable not void, a civil officer cannot lawfully remove him from that service to punish previous desertion; reward cannot be paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward requires delivery to Army officer at convenient post/recruiting station
rubrics_metrics.description: The reward is not due merely on apprehension; there must also be a delivery as prescribed by regulation to an officer of the Army at the most convenient post or recruiting station.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest/releases by State courts can defeat 'delivery' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person arrested is released by a state court (e.g., on habeas corpus) prior to being delivered to military authorities, the arresting police officer may not be entitled to the reward because no valid delivery occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 13958 Jan. 15, 1903; note that subsequent re-arrest may be possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge removes military jurisdiction — no reward
rubrics_metrics.description: If subsequent to the desertion the person was dishonorably discharged, that expulsion from the Army removes military jurisdiction and he is not a deserter within the statute/regulation; no reward can be paid for apprehension and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — administrative mistakes on rolls can preserve rewardability
rubrics_metrics.description: If a soldier was dishonorably discharged but by mistake not dropped from rolls and carried as a deserter at large, and later apprehended as such, technically he may be regarded as charged with desertion and reward may be legally paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reward for civilians discharged without honor (once civilian)
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier discharged without honor on account of desertion later apprehended is a civilian and not a deserter; neither reward nor expenses incurred in his apprehension can be paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reward after a deserter's release (deserter's release invalidates claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deserter was furnished a deserter's release and later apprehended for that desertion, neither reward nor expenses can be paid for his apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal defenses to prosecution bar reward
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in view of the limitation of the relevant article (the one hundred and third article), the soldier has a legal defense to prosecution for desertion, the reward is not payable for his apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: P. 55, 264 Sept. 1892; C. 16172 Apr. 12, 1904; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigated payment when statute of limitations has run
rubrics_metrics.description: If after delivery it is discovered that the statute of limitations has run, policy is that the full reward should not be paid; only fair remuneration for the officer's time and reimbursement for actual expenses should be paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat wartime desertion differently for limitation and reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Desertion that occurred during conditions of war (e.g., Philippines before proclamation of peace) is not barred by statute of limitations and reward may be paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal apprehension (violation of foreign sovereignty) bars reward
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deserter was arrested on foreign soil in violation of the territorial rights of that sovereignty (e.g., Mexico), the reward could not be paid, as an illegal act cannot form the basis of a legal claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reward where extradition occurred on other charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Reward should not be paid where a deserter was extradited from another country on charges other than desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender to recruiting officer generally negates reward but reimburses expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deserter surrenders to a recruiting officer who then directs delivery to a military post, a police officer who transports him is not entitled to the authorized reward but may be reimbursed for expenses from the appropriation for apprehension and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender in transit negates status as fugitive for reward purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter who surrenders to a recruiting officer and is being transported to report, if arrested in transit, is not a deserter within meaning of law/regulations as a fugitive from military justice; arresting officer not entitled to reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation term 'citizen' means 'civilian' excluding military reward claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriations for payment of rewards for apprehension of deserters use 'citizen' synonymously with 'civilian' to distinguish civil persons from officers or enlisted men; thus meant to preclude officers/enlisted men from obtaining reward for apprehension without request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited reward eligibility for certain civil officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil officials (e.g., customs officer who lacks general arrest authority; justices of the peace who are not peace officers under state law) may not be entitled to reward absent statutory/request authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 44 Apr. 1891 (customs officer); P. 57 Dec. 1892 (Idaho justice of peace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold reward where evidence of collusion exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The reward should be withheld where there is evidence of collusion between alleged deserter and the civil official delivering him (suspicion of arrangement to obtain reward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where quick voluntary surrender at or near post suggested collusion: P. U, 64 and 100 Nov. 1890; C. 15592 Dec. 10, 1903.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient indicia of desertion negates reward (short absence/uniform)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a soldier when arrested had been absent only a short time, was still in uniform, had not been reported/dropped as deserting, and commander lacked conclusive evidence of intent not to return, there is insufficient evidence to justify payment of reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of desertion at arrest precludes reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil officers who apprehend suspects without knowledge they were deserters (e.g., arrested as suspects for other reasons) are not entitled to the reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: No recovery for one who acts ignorant of the offer
rubrics_metrics.description: One who performs an act for which a reward is offered, but in ignorance of the offer, cannot recover the reward (e.g., merchant turned over man as vagrant not knowing he was a deserter).

rubrics_metrics.name: No compensation for civil officers' mistakes (wrong arrests)
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil officer who, without request, arrests a person as a deserter who was not charged and not actually a deserter cannot be compensated for time/expenses and cannot shift burden to Government for his mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 20 Mar. 1866; multiple Comptroller rulings 1901-1911 cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reimbursement for liability from wrongful arrest judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no provision in appropriations for reimbursement of officers who incur liability by reason of mistakes in identity (whether due to lack of due care or not); claims for such reimbursement cannot be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19263 Feb. 28, 1906 (example where officer obtained judgment against him).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-surrender or technical delivery may not merit reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where the deserter voluntarily surrenders or indicates intention to surrender (policeman arrests on that basis or deputy learns identity from letter) often do not justify a reward claim, especially if the reward offer has been withdrawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration to duty without trial permits reenlistment
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter restored to duty without trial who thereafter serves faithfully may be reenlisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple enlistments and liability to serve
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier deserts from one regiment and enlists in another, he may be held to serve out both enlistments or either; the Government may abandon the first enlistment by discharging him without honor and hold him to the second — no transfer necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting and deserter status unaffected
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter at large who is drafted and serves as a drafted soldier has his status as a deserter unaffected by being drafted or by such service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's discretion to permit reenlistment after dishonorable discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: It is within the power of the Secretary of War to decide, on facts presented, that prior service was honest and faithful and to permit reenlistment even though prior sentence included dishonorable discharge for desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank appointment vacated when dropped from rolls as deserter
rubrics_metrics.description: Dropping a soldier as a deserter on morning reports operates to vacate appointments (e.g., first-class private); erroneous taking-up later does not restore prior appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity discovered in deserter during examination — discharge without honor
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deserter examined pursuant to regulations is found insane and insanity was contracted not in line of duty and while in desertion, the Secretary of War should issue a discharge without honor rather than order commitment to Government Hospital for the Insane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary rule — charge is not proof of desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere charge that a soldier deserted does not constitute proof that he committed the offense; formal evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative records entries not conclusive proof of desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries on morning-report books, descriptive lists, or official returns stating a soldier deserted are not legal evidence proving the offense but only evidence he was charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muster-roll extracts/adjutant reports insufficient standing alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Extracts from muster rolls in reports (e.g., Adjutant General's office) are insufficient proof of the fact of desertion to justify conviction; supporting evidence required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness testimony must state facts, not legal conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness (e.g., first sergeant) should state facts and circumstances known, not simply conclude the accused 'deserted'; such conclusory statements are insufficient to establish the offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dropping from rolls is not legal evidence of desertion at trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier being dropped from the rolls as a deserter is not, by that entry alone, legal evidence to prove desertion upon his trial for the offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior service/other branch enlistment does not affect amenability to trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Amenability to trial of a deserter from an enlistment in the Army is not affected by the fact that when he enlisted he was a deserter from the Marine Corps; prior enlistments may be voidable, not void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of enlistment evidence unnecessary unless alleged
rubrics_metrics.description: In trials for desertion it is not necessary to introduce evidence as to the date of enlistment unless the date is alleged in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistreatment, homesickness, foreign military notice — not absolute defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of ill treatment, lack of food, nostalgia (homesickness), or notification to report for foreign military duty are matters of extenuation but generally not defenses to a charge of desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 34, 411 Aug. 1873; R. 28, 496 Apr. 1869; other citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration to duty without trial by competent authority is a complete answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration to duty without trial, when sanctioned and performed by competent authority, is a complete answer to a subsequent charge of desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power as relief for severe civil disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief from severe civil disabilities (forfeiture of citizenship rights under R.S. sections) caused by desertion convictions has commonly been granted by exercise of the pardoning power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 5280 Nov. 10, 1898; several later cases citing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased punishment for prior desertions not limited to current enlistment
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive order providing maximum punishment that increases for each previous desertion is not limited to desertions occurring in the current enlistment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penitentiary confinement rules when desertion combined with other offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A general prisoner convicted only of desertion cannot be confined in a penitentiary by reason of prohibitions, but if convicted of desertion and other offenses that carry penitentiary punishment, penitentiary confinement may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial timing/punishment limits after war
rubrics_metrics.description: If a soldier deserted in war but was brought to trial after the end of the war (in peace), statute of limitations may not run, but punishment may not exceed that set by the Executive order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desertion includes AWOL; trial outcomes interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Every desertion in which the deserter leaves station before surrender/apprehension includes an absence without leave; on a trial for desertion the accused is also tried for the AWOL involved; acquittal of desertion without reservation acquits as to the lesser offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 33, 123 July 1872; C. 9528 Jan. 13, 1901; multiple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and procedure for restoration to duty without trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter surrendered may be restored to duty without trial where circumstances commend him; application for restoration should be made by company commander and restoration to duty in fraudulent enlistment cases is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture/withholding of pay requires satisfactory ascertainment of desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Forfeiture of pay and allowances for deserters can be imposed only upon satisfactory ascertainment of the fact of desertion — typically by approved conviction by court-martial though may be administratively established (e.g., restoration to duty without trial by competent authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 7 Feb./Mar. 1864; C. 4937 Sept. 1898; C. 7232 Nov. 1, 1899; supervisory Pay Dept. procedure described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disapproved convictions preclude forfeiture of pay/allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewing authority disapproves a conviction on the sole ground that evidence does not sustain the charge, the soldier cannot legally be subjected to forfeiture of pay and allowances as he cannot be treated as a deserter in law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order directing discharge without honor justifies withholding pay
rubrics_metrics.description: An order directing discharge without honor on account of desertion suffices to justify the Pay Department in withholding pay and allowances due at the time charged with desertion.
